This is the Quarto module of the [companion curriculum](index.qmd), and it is optional. It is written for someone who has worked through [getting started with R](intro-r.qmd), or who already writes a little R, and who has never written a Quarto document. Section 2 of that module named the three surfaces into which you type R and described the third, a Quarto document that holds prose and code in a single file, in one paragraph. This page shows how to write one. By the end you will know what a `.qmd` file contains, what rendering does to it, how the header decides what kind of document comes out, how a handful of options control what your reader is shown, how figures and tables acquire captions and numbers, how citations are drawn from a bibliography file, and how a folder of documents becomes a project with settings held in common.

In the courses, the module is the companion of Part 4 of the [one-day course on data tools](../tracks/housing-one-day-data-tools/part-4.qmd), in which you write the value of the reproduction that you chose into the report of the workspace as inline code and render the report from a clean session, and of the last session of day 2 in the three-day courses, which writes up the reproduced value in the report of the workspace, as on the [immigration-and-trust case](../tracks/trust-three-days/day-2.qmd). The self-study track reads sections 1 to 6 in [stage 2](../tracks/self-study/stage-2.qmd) and comes back to sections 7 and 8 in [stage 12](../tracks/self-study/stage-12.qmd).

Every block below is **displayed without being run**. The R module could send you to the zero-install [browser lab](../cases/housing/lab.qmd) to try its code, but this one cannot, because the lab runs R inside a browser tab and does not render documents, as [section 5.1 of the IDE module](ide.qmd#sec-lab) explains. The exercises on this page therefore assume the workspace described on the [setup page](../setup.qmd), with R and an IDE (Positron, RStudio, VS Code, etc.) on your own machine. They also need the Quarto command-line tool, so if `R/check_setup.R` reports a FAIL on its Quarto line, install Quarto from <https://quarto.org> and reopen your terminal. You can read the page without any of that installed, since everything it describes can be found in files that you can open.

The examples come from two projects. The first is the workspace of the housing-audit case, whose report `index.qmd` you fill in during the exercise. The second is this site, whose pages, slide decks and browser lab are all `.qmd` files in one repository. Every claim below can therefore be checked against the file that it came from, including the page you are reading, which is an unusual Quarto document in one respect that [section 3](#sec-chunks) explains.

## 1. Source and output {#sec-what}

A `.qmd` file is plain text, editable in anything, and it holds three kinds of content.

The **YAML header** comes first, fenced above and below by a line of three hyphens. It holds metadata: the title, the author, and above all the output format. The **prose** is Markdown, the lightweight convention in which `##` opens a second-level heading and `**text**` sets text in bold. The **code chunks** are blocks of R (or Python, or Julia) that are executed while the document is being built, with their results placed into the finished document at the point where the chunk stands in the source.

Here is a complete document with all three, short enough to read in one go:

````markdown
---
title: "A first report"
format: html
---

## What the data hold

The housing-audit data hold one row per email.

```{r}
audit <- readr::read_csv("data/housing_audit.csv")
nrow(audit)
```
````

**Rendering** is what turns that file into a document, and two programs do it in sequence. First knitr reads through the file, hands each chunk to R and collects whatever comes back (printed values, warnings, tables, figures), writing out a plain Markdown file with those results pasted in place of the code that produced them. Then Pandoc, a document converter, takes that Markdown and produces the finished artefact, which may be an HTML page, a PDF, a Word file or a set of slides. Because the code runs before any typesetting happens, an error in a chunk halts the render, and no output appears at all, not even the part of the document before the error. Quarto names the chunk that failed when it stops, which is the first reason to give every chunk a label.

Three commands cover ordinary use. `quarto render index.qmd` builds one file. `quarto render` builds every file in a project. `quarto preview` builds the document, opens it in your browser and rebuilds it every time you save, which is how most people work. The README of the workspace puts `quarto preview` at step 5 of getting started, and the setup check in that workspace, `R/check_setup.R`, tests whether Quarto is on your PATH (the list of folders in which your system looks for programs) and points you at <https://quarto.org> if it is missing.

The workspace holds the same analysis twice, once as a script and once as a document. `working_script.R` takes Tasks 1 to 5 as a plain R script that you step through in the console: it checks the setup, counts the emails and draws the causal graph, reproduces the analysis of whichever of the five Multi100 analysts you choose, tries several specifications with `try_spec()`, and reports the one that you fix in your preregistration with `report_result()`. `index.qmd` is the same work as a report, with the reasoning written around the code and the results printed beside the sentences that discuss them. The script is quicker to experiment with. The report is the thing that you can hand to somebody, and its results cannot go stale, because they are recomputed from the data every time that the file is rendered.

It follows that you should never edit the rendered output. The `.html` file is disposable and is rebuilt from the source on demand, so the `.qmd` is the artefact that you keep, version and share.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try it

Download the workspace from the [setup page](../setup.qmd) and open the folder in your IDE. Open `index.qmd`, and in the terminal run `quarto preview`. The report opens in a browser with every chunk executed. Now change one word of the prose and save, and the preview reloads by itself. Then look inside the `_site` folder that has appeared in the workspace and open the `index.html` that you find there. You could edit it, but any change you made would be overwritten at the next render.
:::

## 2. The YAML header {#sec-yaml}

The header of the exercise report is a good one to learn from, because it uses most of the keys that ordinary work needs:

```yaml
---
title: "Testing the robustness of a published claim: the housing-audit case"
author: "Pair: [names]"
date: today
format:
  html:
    toc: true
    toc-depth: 2
    code-fold: false
    df-print: paged
execute:
  message: false
  warning: false
knitr:
  opts_chunk:
    fig-width: 8
    fig-height: 5
---
```

Take it key by key. `title` and `author` print at the top of the finished document. `date: today` is a keyword of Quarto that fills in the date at render time, so a report rendered next month shows the date of next month without anybody remembering to change it. Everything under `format:` configures the HTML output. `toc: true` builds a table of contents from the headings, and `toc-depth: 2` keeps it to the first two heading levels. `code-fold: false` shows code blocks open, where `true` would put each one behind a control that the reader clicks to expand, and `df-print: paged` renders a data frame as a small paged table instead of a block of console text. The `execute:` block sets options for every chunk in the document at once, here suppressing the start-up messages of packages and the warnings that would otherwise clutter a report meant for a reader. The `knitr:` block passes options directly to knitr, here fixing every figure at eight inches by five unless a chunk asks for something else.

`format:` is the one key that changes what kind of document comes out, and the same source can serve several. Every page on this site is `html`. The slide decks are `revealjs`, configured in `slides/_metadata.yml` rather than in the decks themselves, for reasons that [section 7](#sec-project) comes to. The browser labs are `live-html`, a format added by an extension, which is what lets R run inside the browser tab of the reader. Adding `pdf` or `docx` under `format:` gives you those as well, from the same file, without changing a line of the content.

YAML is fussy in a small number of ways, and a malformed header is the most common reason why a document that rendered yesterday will not render today. Indentation is by spaces, never tabs, and two spaces per level is the convention. Every entry is `key: value` with a space after the colon. A string that contains a colon has to be quoted, which is why the title above sits inside quotation marks. Booleans are lower-case `true` and `false`. If a render fails with a message about the YAML, read the header before you read anything else.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try it

In the workspace report, change `toc-depth: 2` to `3` and render again, watching the table of contents grow. Then set `code-fold: true` and look again. Most chunks are now folded behind a small "Code" control, but the setup chunk at the top still shows nothing at all. Work out why from its options before reading the next section, which gives the answer.
:::

## 3. Code chunks and their options {#sec-chunks}

A chunk opens with three backticks and the name of the engine in braces. Its options follow as comment lines beginning `#|`, then comes the code, and a closing fence of three backticks ends it. The option lines are YAML again, so the same rules about colons and spaces apply. This is the first chunk of Task 2 in the exercise report, which counts the emails and what came back:

````markdown
```{r}
#| label: count-emails
# How many emails, and what came back?
audit |>
  datawizard::data_summary(emails    = n(),
                           bounced   = sum(is.na(reply)),
                           delivered = sum(!is.na(reply)),
                           replies   = sum(reply %in% 1),
                           coded     = sum(!is.na(named)))
```
````

It runs, its code is shown, and its result appears underneath: 1,014 emails, of which 23 bounced, 991 were delivered, 563 drew a reply, and 558 replies carry a greeting code. That is the default behaviour, and chunk options are the way to change it. Seven of them cover almost everything that the report and this site need:

| Option | What it does |
|---|---|
| `label` | Names the chunk. Required for cross-references, and Quarto prints it when a chunk fails. |
| `eval: false` | The code is shown but not run. |
| `echo: false` | The code runs and its results appear; the code itself is hidden. |
| `output: false` | The code runs and is shown; its results are hidden. |
| `include: false` | The code runs; neither the code nor its results appear anywhere. |
| `error: true` | An error in the chunk is printed in the document instead of halting the render. |
| `message: false`, `warning: false` | Hide the messages and warnings that R emits while the chunk runs. |

`echo`, `output` and `include` are the three that are most easily confused. `echo` governs the code, `output` governs the results, and `include` is the switch that turns both off while still running the chunk. The exercise report uses `include: false` on its setup chunk, which reads the housing-audit data as `audit` and loads the helpers of Tasks 4 and 5 from `R/spec_tools.R`. That work has to happen before anything else, and no reader needs to see it. This also answers the exercise above, since a chunk that is not included cannot be folded, because it is not in the document at all.

`eval: false` marks a chunk that is printed as an instruction to the reader and never executed. The report uses it for the step that sends your exploratory result to the class chart:

````markdown
```{r}
#| label: submit-exploration
#| eval: false
submit_exploration()
```
````

The reader sees what to run, and rendering the report never sends a submission. `error: true` does the opposite job. In Task 4 the report deliberately asks for an option that is not on the curve, so that you can read the reason why it is refused:

````markdown
```{r}
#| label: try-off-curve
#| error: true
try_spec(model = "three_group")          # all three groups in one model: refused, with the reason why
```
````

Without `error: true` the refusal would stop the render. With it, the message is printed in the report and the render carries on to the next chunk.

Two further options are used on this site. `results: asis` tells Quarto that what the chunk prints is Markdown to be interpreted rather than console text to be shown in a grey box; the toggle that puts the notice of the next delivery on the opening page of the site, in `_includes/next-delivery.qmd`, works that way, printing a callout as text and having Quarto render it. And `fig-width` and `fig-height`, set on a single chunk, override whatever the header set for the document as a whole.

### Where options are set

The same options can be written on a chunk, in the header of a document under `execute:`, in a `_metadata.yml` file that governs a whole folder, or in the configuration of the project. Where an option is set at more than one level, the setting nearest to the chunk wins, and all four levels are in use across the course. The chunks quoted above set their own options. The exercise report suppresses messages and warnings for the whole document. The shared settings of the slide decks, in `slides/_metadata.yml`, set `echo: false`, so no slide ever displays the code behind its figure. And the configuration of the site sets `freeze: auto`, which [section 7](#sec-project) explains.

### Inline code

Code is not confined to chunks. An expression written between backticks and prefixed with `r` is evaluated during the render, and its value is dropped into the sentence. The case study writes that "The `` `r counts$bounced` `` bounced emails never reached an official", so the number in the sentence is counted from the data when the page is built. The [audit-experiments module](experiments.qmd#sec-randomisation) reports that the six names were sent between `` `r sent_range[1]` `` and `` `r sent_range[2]` `` times, and the R module gives the gap among all delivered emails as `` `r fmt(gap_all, 2)` `` points, so neither figure is ever copied out of the console by hand. Part 4 of the one-day course on data tools asks you for one such sentence in the report of the workspace, under the chunk of the analyst whom you reproduced in Task 3: `` `r round(chisq.test(tab_8ptrz)$statistic, 3)` `` gives the value of 8PTRZ, and `` `r round(prop.test(counts_25n5d$greetings, counts_25n5d$emails)$statistic, 3)` `` that of 25N5D.

The habit is worth adopting for anything numeric that you would otherwise type. A number pasted into the text is correct on the day on which it is pasted, and it becomes wrong without any warning as soon as the data, the sample or the model changes. An inline expression is recomputed at every render, so it cannot fall out of step with the analysis.

### Unexecuted chunks

This page is full of chunks that are displayed and never executed, and making that work requires knowing how Pandoc and knitr each read a fence. Pandoc closes a fenced block only at a fence at least as long as the one that opened it, so wrapping a three-backtick chunk in a **four**-backtick fence is enough to make Pandoc treat the inner block as literal text. It is not enough for knitr. Knitr scans the file line by line for a line that opens with backticks followed by `{r}`, and it does not track whether that line sits inside a longer fence, so it finds the inner chunk and runs it anyway. On a page like this one, where the displayed code refers to objects that do not exist, the render then fails.

There are two ways out, and which one you want depends on the page.

If the page has no live code at all, declare `engine: markdown` in the header. Quarto then skips the execution stage entirely, Pandoc handles the fences correctly, and a four-backtick fence displays whatever is inside it. That is what this page does, and it has two side benefits: the page renders without R installed, and it never enters the cache that [section 7](#sec-project) describes. The R module is the opposite case. It runs its code, and where it shows a block that must not run, such as the line that installs a package, it marks that chunk `eval: false`.

If the page does run code and you also want to display a chunk as it is written in the source, double the braces. A fence written as ```` ```{{{r}}} ```` does not match the pattern that knitr looks for, so the block is left alone; one layer of braces is then removed on the way out, and your reader is shown ```` ```{r} ````:

`````markdown
````markdown
```{{{r}}}
#| label: fig-demo
mean(1:10)
```
````
`````

The fence lengths in that example are the same trick applied twice over, five backticks around four around three, because the block being displayed is itself a displayed block. The doubling rule extends to the shortcodes of Quarto, which [section 5](#sec-prose) comes to.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try it

In the workspace report, add `#| echo: false` to the chunk labelled `count-emails` and render again. The counts are still there and the code that produced them is gone, as it is in most published reports. Then swap it for `#| eval: false` and render again, and the code is back while the counts have vanished. Finally, break the chunk on purpose by misspelling `data_summary`, render, and read the error message, noticing that it names the label.
:::

## 4. Captions, labels and cross-references {#sec-crossref}

A figure produced by a chunk becomes a numbered, captioned figure that the prose can refer to once two conditions are met: the chunk has a `fig-cap`, and its label begins with `fig-`. The exercise report draws its figure of the greetings by name that way, with one bar for each of the six names:

````markdown
```{r}
#| label: fig-names
#| fig-cap: "Replies that greeted the sender by name, by the name that signed the email."
#| fig-height: 3.6
greeted <- audit |>
  datawizard::data_filter(!is.na(named)) |>
  datawizard::data_summary(greeted_pct = 100 * mean(named), by = c("group", "name"))

tinyplot::tinyplot(greeted_pct ~ name | group, data = greeted, type = "barplot", flip = TRUE)
```
````

The excerpt leaves out the order of the bars, their colours and the labels, which the report adds. The size option overrides the height of five inches that the header set, because six bars need less room than a scatterplot does. Tables work in the same way, with a `tbl-cap` and a label beginning `tbl-`. The case study captions its table of email counts "The emails in the public file." and gives it the label `tbl-counts`, so it is numbered and can be referred to in the same way.

With the prefix in place, Quarto numbers the item and lets you point at it from the prose. Write `@fig-names` in a sentence and the rendered text reads "Figure 1", as a link that takes the reader to it. The report already has three labelled figures, `fig-names`, `fig-dag` and `fig-curve`, and nothing yet refers to them, so adding a reference is a one-word edit that shows the whole mechanism working.

Sections can be cross-referenced in the same way, with an id beginning `sec-` attached to the heading in braces, but numbered section references need `number-sections: true` in the header. The pages of this site are not numbered, so they use those same ids as plain anchor links instead. The R module writes `[section 3](#sec-objects)` to point within itself, and the audit-experiments module writes `[causal-graphs module](dags.qmd#sec-case)` to point at a section of another page. Both are ordinary Markdown links, and a link to a heading in another file takes no more effort to write than a link to one in the same file.

A figure that comes from an image file uses the image syntax of Markdown, `![A caption](path/to/image.png){#fig-example}`, and it is numbered and referred to in the same way. The course uses that syntax rarely, for a diagram such as the one of the rendering pipeline in the slides on the toolchain. Its charts are drawn by chunks from the data files, so that a chart can be corrected and drawn again whenever the data change.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try it

In the workspace report, find the sentence below the figure chunk in Task 2 and rewrite it so that it refers to `@fig-names`. Render again and check that the caption now begins "Figure 1" and that your reference links to it. Then change the label of that chunk to `names-figure`, dropping the prefix, and render once more. The caption survives, the number disappears, and your cross-reference prints as `?@fig-names`, which is how Quarto reports a reference that it cannot resolve.
:::

## 5. Markdown {#sec-prose}

The writing between the chunks is Markdown, with a few additions made by Quarto. Headings are lines beginning with one to six `#` characters. Emphasis is `*italic*` and `**bold**`. Lists are lines beginning with `-`, or with `1.` where the items should be numbered. A link is `[the visible text](the-target)`, and a link between pages of a Quarto site points at the **source** file rather than the rendered one: this page links to the R module as `[getting started with R](intro-r.qmd)`, and Quarto rewrites the target to `intro-r.html` when it builds the site. Writing `.qmd` targets means that a link keeps working if the output format changes, and that Quarto can warn you when a target does not exist.

The addition that you will use most is the **fenced div**, a block of content wrapped between two lines of colons, with a class in braces on the opening line. It is a general mechanism for marking a region of a document as being of a particular kind, and callouts are the instance that you meet everywhere. This is the Task 3 box of the exercise report, shortened here to two of its sentences and two of the five tabs that it holds, one for each analyst whose analysis you can choose to reproduce:

````markdown
::::: {.callout-note title="Task 3 – The reproduction"}
This is the **reproducibility** check. **Choose one of the five** and reproduce the analysis from the public file of the OAs, `audit_original.csv`.

::: {.panel-tabset}

### 8PTRZ

Hispanic names against all other names, with a chi-square test of the 2 × 2 table.

### UYV3F

Hispanic against white names only, with a logistic regression.

:::

:::::
````

Five callout classes ship with Quarto: `note`, `tip`, `important`, `caution` and `warning`, each with its own colour and icon. The five tasks of the exercise report are `.callout-note` boxes with a `title` attribute, the box that explains how the tasks work is a `.callout-tip`, like the "Try it" boxes on this page, and the note that maps the preregistration block onto a real preregistration form is a `.callout-important`. Adding `collapse="true"` starts a callout closed, with a control that the reader clicks to open it. The report uses it for two asides, on the five analysts and on the difference between exploratory and declared results, which would otherwise interrupt the flow of a task.

Divs nest, and when they do, the outer one takes more colons than the inner. The Task 3 box holds a div of the class `.panel-tabset`, which turns each heading inside it into a tab, so the box opens and closes with five colons and the tabset with three. Forgetting the extra colons can leave one box swallowing the rest of the page.

Two **shortcodes** appear across this site, each written as a name inside doubled braces and angle brackets. `{{{< var name >}}}` inserts a value from `_variables.yml`, the single file that holds facts used across the site, so the address of the workspace repository of each case is written once there, under the key `cases`, and referred to everywhere else by that key, as `{{{< var cases.housing.template-repo >}}}` for the housing-audit case, in the browser lab and in the git module among other places. The cheatsheet takes the address of the site and the download link of the workspace from the same file. `{{{< include path >}}}` pastes another file into this one before rendering, which is how the browser lab picks up the setup code of the extension that runs R in the browser, and how each deck is assembled from its segments. Both keep a fact or a block of markup in a single file, so that it cannot differ from one page to the next.

Displaying a shortcode without running it needs the same brace-doubling that [section 3](#sec-chunks) described for chunks, and it is easy to forget the first time. Every shortcode in the paragraph above is written in the source of this page with three braces on each side, because Quarto strips one layer and would otherwise have run them, and the sentence would have printed the address of the repository where it meant to show you the markup.

## 6. Citations {#sec-citations}

Add a `bibliography:` key to the header, pointing at a BibTeX file, and citations start working. The pages of this site write `bibliography: [../references.bib, ../references-new.bib]`, a list of two files, because the project keeps a second file for entries that are not yet in the reference library of the facilitator. A single file is written without the brackets, and both forms are ordinary YAML.

A BibTeX file is a plain-text database with one record per work. This is the record for the paper behind the housing-audit case, as it stands in `references-new.bib`:

```bibtex
@article{EinsteinGlick2017DoesRaceAffect,
  title = {Does Race Affect Access to Government Services? {{An}} Experiment
           Exploring Street-Level Bureaucrats and Access to Public Housing},
  author = {Einstein, Katherine Levine and Glick, David M.},
  year = {2017},
  journal = {American Journal of Political Science},
  volume = {61},
  number = {1},
  pages = {100--116},
  doi = {10.1111/ajps.12252}
}
```

The word immediately after the opening brace is the **citekey**, the name by which you cite the work. Almost nobody types these records by hand. A reference manager such as Zotero holds the library and exports the file, keys and all, so the practical workflow is to save a paper into the manager once and cite it from every document afterwards.

Four citation forms cover ordinary writing:

| You write | It renders as |
|---|---|
| `[@EinsteinGlick2017DoesRaceAffect]` | a parenthetical citation, authors and year in brackets |
| `@EinsteinGlick2017DoesRaceAffect` | an in-text citation, with only the year bracketed |
| `[@EinsteinGlick2017DoesRaceAffect, p. 100]` | a parenthetical citation with a page locator |
| `[@EinsteinGlick2017DoesRaceAffect; @LundbergEtAl2021WhatYourEstimand]` | two works in one set of brackets |

The reference list is assembled from whatever you actually cited, and it goes at the end of the document unless you say otherwise. Putting `::: {#refs}` somewhere places the list at that point, which is why the modules of this site end with a `## References` heading and an empty div underneath it. This page ends the same way, and the two entries that you will find there were produced by live citations of the two works named in the table above [@EinsteinGlick2017DoesRaceAffect; @LundbergEtAl2021WhatYourEstimand].

Formatting is controlled by a citation style file, written in the Citation Style Language (CSL). No `csl:` key is set on any page of this site, so every page renders in the default that Pandoc supplies, the Chicago author-date style. Pointing `csl:` at a style file from the repository of CSL styles, which Zotero hosts, switches the whole document to APA or to the house style of a particular journal, without touching a single citation.

A bare `@Key` at the very start of a block is also the syntax by which Pandoc writes an example list, and Pandoc reads it that way in preference: the citation disappears and a list number takes its place, with no warning. The slide decks of this course run into that, because their pinned source footers open with a bare citekey so that the names of the authors render outside the brackets. The fix is in `slides/_metadata.yml`, which turns the example-list syntax off with `from: markdown-example_lists`. The same file sets `link-citations: true`, which makes every rendered citation a link to its entry in the list.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try it

The workspace report lists its five references by hand at the bottom of the file, as ordinary prose. Convert it. Make a `references.bib` beside the report, put those five works into it as BibTeX records exported from a reference manager, add `bibliography: references.bib` to the header, replace the hand-typed list with `## References` and an empty `::: {#refs}` div, and cite each work at the point in the report where it is discussed. Render again, and check that all five still appear and that none of them appears twice.
:::

## 7. Projects {#sec-project}

A single `.qmd` renders on its own. Put a `_quarto.yml` file beside it and the folder becomes a **project**: a set of documents that share settings, render together and can be published as one thing. The site you are reading is a project of the type `website`, and the parts of its configuration that matter here are these:

```yaml
project:
  type: website
  output-dir: _site

format:
  html:
    theme: cosmo
    css: styles.css
    toc: true

execute:
  freeze: auto
```

Left out of the excerpt are the list of files to render and the navigation bar, which defines the menus at the top of this page. The `format:` block sets the defaults for every page at once, so no page has to ask for a table of contents or name the visual theme. The workspace is a much smaller project of the same kind: its configuration names the type of project and the title of the site, renders `index.qmd` as its only page, sets `freeze: auto`, and adds `code-tools: true`, so that a reader of the rendered report can open the source behind any chunk.

Settings can also be attached to a single folder by putting a `_metadata.yml` inside it, and every `.qmd` in that folder inherits them. The slide decks are built this way. The header of each deck holds only a few keys: a title, a subtitle, `format: revealjs` and the list of optional runs that the deck includes in its main flow, and in the decks of the housing-audit case a `deck:` key that names the format, so that the segments shared between formats can show or hide a line for each. The theme, the partial (a template fragment) for the title slide, the bibliography, the background and several dozen presentation options are all set in `slides/_metadata.yml` beside them, along with `echo: false`. Four levels are therefore available, and the nearest one wins: an option on a chunk beats the header of the document, which beats the file of the folder, which beats the configuration of the project.

`freeze: auto`, the last setting in that excerpt, tells Quarto, when it renders the whole project, to execute a document again only when its source file has changed, and then to run every chunk in it. The results are stored in a folder called `_freeze/`, one record for each document, and a render of a single file always executes its code. This site commits that folder to version control, so the workflow that publishes the site installs Quarto and then only five R packages before it renders: knitr, rmarkdown and yaml, which run a chunk and read its options, and readr and datawizard, which the code of the opening page calls. Everything else comes out of the cache, which means that the build machine never needs the packages with which the pages were written. The exception is the opening page, which runs with `freeze: false` so that `_variables.yml` is read afresh for the notice of the next delivery on every build, and those five packages are installed for that page alone.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try it

Open `slides/_metadata.yml` in the repository of this site and read it from the top, working out what each block does before you reach the `execute:` block at the bottom. Then open `_quarto.yml` and find two places where a setting is made once for every page of the site.
:::

## 8. Publishing the document {#sec-publish}

Rendering a project writes the finished site to the folder that `output-dir` names, here `_site`. Rendering a single document writes the output beside the source. Either way the result is a set of ordinary files, and publishing means putting them somewhere that other people can reach.

Three routes are common. You can render locally and commit the output, which is the simplest and suits a small document that changes rarely. You can run `quarto publish gh-pages`, a single command that creates a branch for the rendered output and pushes to it. Or you can have a build machine do the work on every change, which is what this site does: its workflow file checks out the repository, installs Quarto and R, renders and deploys the contents of `_site`. The workspace repository has a workflow of its own, `.github/workflows/publish.yml`, which works differently. It installs R together with the twelve packages of the exercise and runs the chunks again, so that a participant who edits the report and pushes it is shown their own results on the published page instead of the ones that shipped.

A document meant to be emailed needs a different setting. `embed-resources: true` places every image, stylesheet and script inside the HTML file itself, giving one self-contained file that works with no folder of assets beside it. The decks of this course set it to `false`, because they are built as part of a site in which those assets are served anyway.

Rendering to PDF is a change to the header, `format: pdf`, plus a typesetting engine. If you have no LaTeX installation, `quarto install tinytex` fetches a small one that Quarto manages itself.

This page stops short of version control, which has a module of its own. Publishing a rendered document is worth little if the source that produced it has no recorded history, and a Quarto project is unusually well suited to being versioned, because its inputs are plain text that can be compared line by line. The [git and GitHub module](git-github.qmd) takes it from there, including what belongs in a repository and what must never enter one. For where a finished analysis should be deposited so that it can be cited and found, the [repositories module](repositories.qmd) covers the archives and their conventions, with the package of the housing-audit case as its example.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try it

Add `docx` under the `format:` key of the workspace report, so that both `html` and `docx` are listed, and run `quarto render`. Two documents appear. Open the Word file and look at what survived the change of format and what did not (the table of contents, the figures, the code blocks, the callout boxes), then decide which format you would give a supervisor and which you would give a co-author who wants to leave comments.
:::

## Sources and further study {#sec-sources}

This module was written for the course and adapts no existing lesson, so there is no borrowed text to attribute. It teaches the part of Quarto that this site and the workspace actually use, illustrated from the files themselves, and it stops well short of the full set of features.

The official documentation is the reference to keep open beside your own document, and these are the pages worth bookmarking first:

- **The Quarto guide**, <https://quarto.org/docs/guide/>, is the starting point for the rest of the documentation, organised by what you are trying to make.
- **Markdown Basics**, <https://quarto.org/docs/authoring/markdown-basics.html>, covers the whole syntax of the prose: headings, emphasis, lists, links, tables, footnotes, divs and spans.
- **Execution Options**, <https://quarto.org/docs/computations/execution-options.html>, covers the chunk options of [section 3](#sec-chunks) in full, and **Code Cells: Knitr**, <https://quarto.org/docs/reference/cells/cells-knitr.html>, is the exhaustive list for R chunks.
- **Cross References**, <https://quarto.org/docs/authoring/cross-references.html>, and **Callout Blocks**, <https://quarto.org/docs/authoring/callouts.html>, document the two features of [sections 4](#sec-crossref) and [5](#sec-prose) beyond what is used here.
- **Citations**, <https://quarto.org/docs/authoring/citations.html>, covers bibliographies, citation syntax and style files.
- **Quarto Projects**, <https://quarto.org/docs/projects/quarto-projects.html>, and **Managing Execution**, <https://quarto.org/docs/projects/code-execution.html>, explain the configuration of projects and the freeze mechanism of [section 7](#sec-project).
- **GitHub Pages**, <https://quarto.org/docs/publishing/github-pages.html>, sets out the three publishing routes of [section 8](#sec-publish) with worked examples of each.

Within this curriculum, the natural neighbours are [getting started with R](intro-r.qmd), which this module assumes, and the [git and GitHub module](git-github.qmd), which takes the reproducible document into version control. Every other page of the site is also a worked example: open any of them in the repository and you are reading the source of something that you have already read rendered.
